site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: A Name That Saves at Last
body: In his old age, the Brahmin Ajamila had wandered far from his vows, but beside him sat his little son named Narayana, the very name he would soon need most. When the messengers of Yama arrived to claim his failing soul, Ajamila cried out in fear, calling the holy name of Narayana as if it were only his child's.

At once, the messengers of Vishnu appeared and gently forbade the servants of Yama, declaring that even a name spoken without full devotion still carries the power to protect. Ajamila felt shame and wonder rise together as the dark attendants withdrew, leaving his heart quietly rescued.

Given this unexpected mercy, Ajamila left his troubled life behind and journeyed to Prayaga, where he spent his remaining years in sincere service to Vishnu. There, in peaceful devotion, he at last attained liberation, his final breath a soft offering of the name that had saved him.

stories.title: Four Friends Who Set Each Other Free
body: On a quiet stretch of forest, the deer, the crow, the mouse, and the tortoise gathered daily as friends, each bringing a different wisdom from their own way of life. Their bond was simple and sure, until a hunter's snare caught the deer by the leg, and the forest held its breath.

The crow, watching from above, hurried to the mouse, whose small teeth worked quickly at the rope. When the hunter came close, the tortoise rolled toward the river and pretended to quarrel with the waters, buying the precious minutes they needed. With each friend giving what they had, the snare parted and the deer bounded free.

The hunter, seeing the four working together with such trust, turned away with empty hands. One by one, the animals slipped back to their homes beneath the trees, their friendship deepened by what each had given for the other, a small circle of kindness no net could hold.

stories.title: A King Heals With Wisdom
stories.source: Mahabharata · Vana Parva, Tirtha-yatra Parva (Ganguli translation)
body: During the long year of forest wandering after the game of dice, the disguised Pandavas and Draupadi shared a humble home with a kind brahmin family. One morning, tragedy struck when a serpent's bite stole the life of the brahmin's young son, and grief filled the little cottage.

Yudhishthira followed the serpent-king deep into the forest, where instead of drawing a weapon, he met the guardian with calm questions of dharma. Steady and clear, the king answered each one with truth, and the serpent, pleased by such grace, relented.

Together the serpent and the weeping father restored the child to life, and the grateful brahmin bowed low before Yudhishthira. With his family, the king returned to his exile in the forest, carrying the quiet proof that compassion can heal where force cannot.

stories.title: Savitri's Bright Devotion
body: In the forest kingdom of Madra, Princess Savitri heard of Satyavan, the gentle son of a blind exiled king, and learned his life was fated to last only one more year. Without fear, she chose him, telling her father no other bridegroom could take his place, and went to live simply among the trees as his devoted wife.

When the destined day finally arrived, Savitri kept her sacred fast and kept watch beside him. Soon Yama, the god of death himself, came to claim Satyavan's soul. Yet Savitri followed the dark deity through the forest, speaking with such wisdom and loving truth that Yama, step by step, granted her boon after shining boon.

At last, even the lord of death could not refuse her steadfast heart. He returned Satyavan's life, and Savitri brought her husband safely home to the forest hermitage, where their days together continued in quiet joy.

stories.title: Lesson of the Loving Mongoose
body: A pious Brahmin's wife slipped away to the river for water, leaving her infant son asleep on the bed while the faithful house-mongoose stood watch. When a black snake slithered toward the cradle, the little guardian dashed forward, killed the serpent, and hurried to the door with its mouth still stained from the fight.

The Brahmin came home and saw only the blood-flecked face of his trusted friend. Fear overwhelmed him, and in a single desperate moment he struck the mongoose down with a stone, believing he had lost everything he loved most.

Inside, his son cooed safely in the cradle, and beside him lay the dead snake the mongoose had given its life to defeat. Grief bowed the Brahmin low, yet the lesson rose gently within him: to look, to know, and to trust before acting.
